description.value: Orbited Mercury to study its geology, magnetic field, and surface composition. Its measurements also confirmed water ice in deposits near the poles.
Explored Saturn, its rings, and its moons from orbit. Observations revealed methane rivers and seas on Titan and jets of ice and gas from Enceladus.
Visited Vesta and Ceres in the main asteroid belt, spending time in orbit around each. The two worlds offered a comparison between a giant asteroid and a dwarf planet.
Orbited Jupiter for almost eight years and made close passes by its major moons. Its observations provided evidence for an ocean beneath the ice on Europa.
Observes planets, stars, and galaxies from Earth orbit in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light. Its cameras record images, while its spectrographs measure light to study composition.
Studies Jupiter beneath its clouds to understand how the planet formed. Close passes revealed polar storms, deep winds, and volcanic activity on its moon Io.
Flew past Pluto and its moons, then continued to the Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth. These encounters provided the first close views of both distant worlds.
Monitors the Sun’s interior, atmosphere, magnetic field, and energy output. These observations help explain how solar activity develops and how it drives changes in space weather.
Flew past Jupiter and Saturn before crossing into interstellar space. Its journey carried it beyond the heliopause, the boundary of the region dominated by the solar wind.
Explored Jupiter and Saturn, then continued to Uranus and Neptune. It became the only spacecraft to visit those two planets before entering interstellar space in 2018.
Maps the Moon’s terrain and measures its temperature, composition, and radiation environment. The observations help identify landing sites and locate resources near the lunar south pole.
Examines the history of water on Mars using close surface images, mineral measurements, and subsurface observations. It also monitors the atmosphere and helps identify potential landing sites.
Mapped the chemical elements and minerals on the Martian surface. Its observations also record clouds, fog, frost, and surface rocks to support the study and exploration of Mars.
Became the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid when it reached Eros. After a year of observations, it touched down on the surface, also making the first asteroid landing.
Collected rocks and dust from asteroid Bennu and delivered them to Earth in a capsule. The spacecraft then continued toward Apophis under the new mission name OSIRIS-APEX.
Collected material from the surface and subsurface of asteroid Ryugu. It returned the samples to Earth in a capsule, allowing researchers to study them in laboratories.
Traveled to asteroid Itokawa to collect material and return it to Earth. The recovered capsule carried rocky grains that could be examined directly in laboratories.
Followed comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko to study its nucleus and surrounding environment. It also delivered the Philae probe to the surface during its stay at the comet.
Measures interactions between Earth’s land, oceans, atmosphere, and energy balance. Its observations track environmental change and help study natural hazards such as fires and volcanic activity.
Observes clouds, oceans, vegetation, ice, land, and the atmosphere from Earth orbit. The measurements support studies of daily weather conditions and changes in climate over longer periods.
Used radar to map the surface of Venus from orbit. Its observations covered almost the entire planet, revealing terrain hidden beneath the thick cloud cover.
Mapped Mars and studied its atmosphere, surface, and interior. It also identified potential landing sites and relayed data for later missions operating on the surface.
The orbiter of the Viking 1 mission to Mars.
The lander of the Viking 1 mission to Mars.
The orbiter of the Viking 2 mission to Mars.
The lander of the Viking 2 mission to Mars.
Ebb was one of the two lunar gravity-mapping GRAIL spacecraft.
Flow was one of the two lunar gravity-mapping GRAIL spacecraft.
Huygens descended through Titan’s atmosphere and transmitted measurements from its surface.
Galileo’s deployed probe measured Jupiter’s atmosphere and relayed its observations through the orbiter.
The Rosetta mission’s lander carried instruments to study comet 67P from its surface.
Hayabusa carried this small experimental robot for exploring Itokawa.
Hayabusa2 carried MINERVA-II Rover-1A as a small rover for exploring Ryugu.
Hayabusa2 carried MINERVA-II Rover-1B as a small rover for exploring Ryugu.
Hayabusa2 carried MINERVA-II Rover-2 as a small rover for exploring Ryugu.
Hayabusa2 carried MASCOT as a small lander for exploring Ryugu.

Arecibo Observatory’s primary telescope from 1963 until cable failures destroyed it in 2020. Its fixed spherical reflector used line feeds in suspended carriage houses, and it worked as both a radio telescope and a solar system radar.

A fully steerable parabolic radio and radar antenna in the NASA Deep Space Network. It opened in 1964 at 64 m and was extended to 70 m in 1988; it transmits for solar system radar as well as receiving.
Melipal, one of the four 8.2-m Ritchey-Chrétien unit telescopes of ESO’s Very Large Telescope at Paranal in Chile. Its alt-azimuth mount lets it point over the whole sky.
An array of 66 antennas on the Chajnantor plateau in Chile, observing between 0.32 and 3.6 mm. Fifty 12-metre dishes act together as one interferometer, with a compact array alongside them.

A 3.2-m Cassegrain telescope on Mauna Kea built to support the Voyager missions and now the United States national facility for infrared astronomy. At least half its observing time goes to planetary science.
A pointing and scanning infrared observatory in an Earth-trailing solar orbit, with an 85-cm aperture and three cryogenically cooled instruments covering the near- to far-infrared.
